Only by reading through the member signatures can you tell whether a type appears in a parameter, a result, or an interface property.

Early notes treated lines 10, 11, and 16 as a group of "callback entry points", but that label was too broad. They are now recorded separately: line 10 enters the `Cdp` namespace, line 11 provides an integer alias, and line 16 is where we finally reach the `Api` interface. When a search finds a plain `number`, do not automatically label it as `Cdp.integer`; conversely, when you encounter `Cdp.integer`, simply return here to verify its declaration.

export namespace Cdp {

```

src/cdp/api.d.ts

  -> l10n
  -> inject / injectable

This made it convenient to jump from the filenames to several common dependencies, but it incorrectly turned "co-located in the header" into "happening sequentially." The decorator and injection marker do appear in adjacent imports, but no constructor arguments were retained, so this alone cannot show where the resolver obtains the object or where the object flows afterward.

A later review confirmed only the following adjacency:

```ts

import { promises as fs } from 'fs';
import { inject, injectable } from 'inversify';
import * as path from 'path';
```

First confirm the classes, functions, and parameters declared in the resolver; when you encounter `fs`, extract the actual member name; when you encounter `path`, record the relevant expression; when you encounter `l10n`, check which branch it is near. # CDP Stream and Content Mapping Decision

Set the boundary first: trace mapping only receives content that has already been read; it is not responsible for rereading failed resources. The meeting considered two options: have mapping content compensate for a direct HTTP failure, or finish the transport read before handing off. The decision is the latter; content does not serve as the end signal for HTTP.

If a direct HTTP resource request fails, we must switch to a CDP Network/IO stream, advance offset by the UTF-8 byte count rather than the UTF-16 character count, and close the stream when Content-Length is reached, retaining status and body.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> DirectHTTP
    DirectHTTP --> CDPStream: request failed
    CDPStream --> Complete: UTF-8 offset reaches Content-Length
    Complete --> [*]: preserve status and body
```

The earlier character-count assessment is no longer valid. `src/cdp/api.d.ts` is the current interface entry point; DBG-201 and DBG-217 remain pointers for further investigation into where resources transition to streams and where legacy calls enter mapping. Caching and replacement are outside this page's scope. When that failed direct request is handed to Network.loadNetworkResource, the options object must include includeCredentials because LoadNetworkResourceOptions in src/cdp/api.d.ts requires that boolean property. The interface types the field as a boolean. It does not fix the value, and this decision does not choose true or false.

# Hot-reload replacement and empty-target termination proposal

When hot reload discovers the same compiled source again, the stored source instance may already have been replaced, but it's unclear whether the old object retrieved earlier will still be used. An empty target receiving another termination request has a similar issue: Fang Ke is called to return early, but that doesn't mean the shutdown entry point has received the request.

We'll start by trying two focused approaches this round. On the source side, compare "overwriting directly after discovering a new instance" with "adopting the new instance first, then checking old references separately"; on the termination side, compare "having the caller return when the target is empty" with "letting the request continue to the termination entry point, where repeated calls are absorbed." Source maps, remote sources, breakpoint resolution, and port reconnection are out of scope for this round.

The tentative preference is for the second source approach, because overwriting the storage location isn't the same as cleaning up the old relationships. On the termination side, we also need to know whether the second request advances shutdown again; we can't just look at whether the caller reports an error.

Withdrawal conditions: If replacement requires invalidating the container first, or if old references can only be cleaned up by unrelated callers on their own, stop at mapping the relationships. Open questions: whether work that has already obtained the old source continues using the original object during replacement; what minimum result repeated termination needs to leave behind.
versions.change_summary: Documented two focused approaches to try

# Hot-Reload Replacement and Termination Without a Target

The initial draft reduced the situation to two very short actions: overwrite the current storage location after rediscovering the compiled source, and have the caller return early if there is no target. This made it easy to start investigating, but hid two handoff issues. Overwriting changes only one stored association; work that already holds the old source will not automatically switch to reading the new object. An early return only means that one call site stops proceeding; it does not show how the termination entry point handles repeated requests.

## Scope for this round

This round still covers only the same compiled source reappearing and re-entering termination when there is no object to terminate. Source maps, remote sources, breakpoint resolution, and port reconnection remain out of scope for now. They may be adjacent to the debugging process, but the available material does not establish that they belong to these two decision points.

On rediscovery, check three things separately: whether a new instance was created, which storage location subsequent discovery uses to obtain the object, and whether paths that continue reading after replacement get the new object or the old one. Matching paths can help with follow-up checks, but do not by themselves establish that two instances are interchangeable. For termination, compare the object state before the request arrives and whether shutdown advances again after the request passes through the entry point.

## File-related investigation pointers

The old notes link the issue name and call name to `src/adapter/sources.ts`. Near the file header are `import * as l10n from '@vscode/l10n';`, the dependency-injection-related `inject` and `injectable`, `js-xxhash`'s `xxHash32`, and `path`'s `relative`. These only identify nearby areas involving hints, injection, identity clues, and path handling. The import list alone does not establish that the source lifecycle is managed exclusively here.

An old margin note says, "A hash is enough to determine source identity here." This version retains it as a working hypothesis, but no longer treats it as a conclusion. `xxHash32` only shows that identity-related clues are visible; it does not establish the full set of identity rules or that old references are all invalidated here. `relative` likewise only helps explain path handling.

## Candidates after review

Option A still overwrites the current storage location as soon as a new source arrives. Its advantage is that the changes are localized, and subsequent discovery starting there can adopt the new object relatively quickly. The downside is that work already in progress may hold the old instance, and overwriting will not make it read the new object. There is also no separate observation point for when the old association is retired.

Option B separates adoption from retiring the old instance. First make the new instance the object used by subsequent discovery, then confirm that the old instance will no longer be retained in new stored associations. This option makes no upfront commitment that all work already in progress must switch; it only avoids equating "the new object has been registered" with "the old object has been cleared out." The trial currently leans toward B.

The two termination candidates are not entirely symmetric either. Having the caller return immediately is cheap, but leaves multiple call sites to interpret "termination complete" independently. Letting the request continue to the entry point allows a comparison of whether both the first request and repeated requests advance shutdown; the cost is having to leave a decision point near the entry point that can be inspected later. The output format is not specified here yet.

## Recheck addendum

An actual recheck did not produce a single overall "pass" verdict. A new instance being registered while the old association is still retrievable is one failure; the old association being removed but shutdown advancing again is another. The former concerns the source handoff, the latter the termination entry point; they cannot be collapsed into a single status label.

The recheck also overturned the simplified rule, "If the paths match, just reuse the existing instance." Paths remain an entry-point clue, but work that had already obtained the old source provides a counterexample. For termination, "null value skipped" is not used as the sole result either, because the caller no longer proceeding does not establish whether the entry point has received repeated requests.

If the trial requires changes to unrelated callers to clean up old references or prevent a second shutdown, stop there. During replacement, whether work using the old source should run to completion or reread later remains undecided; what needs to be recorded for repeated termination—the call result or the shutdown action—is also left for the next recheck.

# Proposal for Hot-Reload Replacement and Null-Target Termination

This proposal did not begin as a complete lifecycle design. It grew out of two small observed cases: after the same compiled source reappeared, whether the source at the current storage location was already a different object; and what would happen when another termination request arrived after the target was already null. Both involved old state, but one concerned the object relationships of source, while the other concerned the shutdown entry point. The early records did not combine them into a common mechanism.

## The Starting Point in 2023

The initial short note confined the changes to the two locations closest to the observed cases. A new instance was written directly at the source discovery point, and the caller returned early upon finding a null target. The benefits were straightforward: rediscovery immediately provided a current object, and the termination call would not proceed further. The scope narrowed accordingly, observing only one rediscovery and one null-target call, without bringing in source map, remote sources, breakpoint resolution, or port recovery.

The working hypothesis at the time was that once the stored association was rewritten, the old source would naturally cease to matter; once the caller returned, repeated termination would naturally end as well. This judgment did not answer when the handoff occurred. Work that had already obtained the old object might continue to carry it, and the caller might return before reaching the termination entry point. The first draft therefore left only two questions, without presenting them as confirmed behavior: who removes the old object, and who handles the second request.

There was only one early stop condition: if source discovery, target shutdown, and caller state all had to change together, do not expand the proposal further. No reason was given at the time. Looking back, this condition preserved an important constraint—once every caller independently guesses how to clean up the old association, or independently decides whether a null target means termination is complete, the observed cases can no longer be reviewed separately by object and entry point.

## Margin Notes from the Autumn Review

The review began near `src/adapter/sources.ts`. Near the top of the file, `import * as l10n from '@vscode/l10n';` was visible, along with imports of `inject`, `injectable`, `xxHash32`, and `relative`. They indicated nearby locations for hints, dependency injection, identity-related clues, and path handling, respectively, so they could serve as starting points for tracing back. There was not enough evidence here to identify any one import as the sole owner of the source lifecycle.

One margin note at the time read: "There is a hash, so source identity must be determined here." This sentence was later crossed out, but not deleted. It represented an overinterpretation of `xxHash32` at the time. The presence of a hash only showed that identity-related clues were visible nearby; it did not establish the complete identity rules, much less imply that all old references would be removed at the same location. `relative` was also only a clue about path handling; the same path could help locate rediscovery, but was not enough to prove that two source instances could be directly interchanged.

The review laid out two candidates for the source side. Option A was to overwrite the current storage location immediately after a new source arrived. This appeared to be a small change, and subsequent discovery starting from that storage location could adopt the new object relatively quickly. The problem was that paths where work had already started might have obtained the old instance earlier, and overwriting the storage location would not automatically change the objects held by that work.

Option B treated "adopting the new instance" and "removing the old association" separately. The new instance would first become the object used by subsequent discovery, and the old instance would then be checked separately to see whether it was still retained in new stored associations. Option B did not claim that all work already started had to reread immediately, nor did it require a complete list of all readers in this round. It only rejected equating registration of the new instance with cleanup of the old association.

The termination side did not copy the treatment of the source side. An early return by the caller could save a step, but would give each call site its own interpretation of "termination complete." Allowing the request to continue to the termination entry point would make it possible to observe whether a repeated request advanced shutdown again. The review did not settle the code structure inside the entry point, but only required distinguishing two cases: a request that arrived without shutting down again, and a request that was skipped upstream.

A short note beside the meeting notes read: "Overwriting is not cleanup." Another read: "A null target is not exempt from termination semantics." Neither was an implementation instruction, but they explained why the review could not simply compare a Boolean result. Both notes remain here as the reason the observation points were later separated.

## Review Record: The First Counterexample

The subsequent review first followed the stored associations of source to examine rediscovery, then looked back at paths that continued reading after replacement. The records did not establish an overall result. The new instance had entered the current storage location, but some work that had already started might still hold the old object; this showed that completed registration was no substitute for removing old references. On the other hand, even if the old association was no longer retained as a new stored association, that still did not establish that work already started had to be interrupted or reread.

This counterexample undermined the claim that "immediate overwriting is enough," but did not prove that all read paths had to switch in sync. It only tightened the proposal's description: which object subsequent discovery should use, and how work that had already obtained the old object should finish, had to be recorded separately. If the material only showed a change at the storage location, it could not be described as complete replacement.

The termination side showed the same kind of discrepancy. A null value could stop the caller from continuing, but if the first request had already entered shutdown and the second request merely returned somewhere else, the records still would not show whether the termination entry point advanced shutdown again. Therefore, "no exception" was not a sufficient observation point; it was necessary to see whether the shutdown action advanced repeatedly.

This review also retained an incomplete record of an observed case: source replacement and target shutdown might occur close together in the same debugging session, but there was no evidence that they shared a state object. The proposal did not include the state queue, Context Shutdown Order, or transport recovery among its decisions. They would enter the corresponding investigation only when a specific entry point showed an effect.

## The Retained Old Approach (Deprecated)

> Old approach: compiled sources with the same path directly reuse the existing source; when the target is null, the caller skips termination.

This passage is retained verbatim and marked as deprecated. It once made investigation quick: compare paths first, then find the overwrite point; the caller returns upon seeing a null value. Paths are still useful for finding entry points, and a null target may still end a particular call early, but the old approach did not record whether a new instance was created, did not record work that had obtained the old object before replacement, and did not record whether the termination entry point received the request.

The old approach also contained a confusion that surfaced later. It understood both source replacement and target shutdown as "skipping the old state," collapsing stored associations, object references, caller returns, and shutdown actions into a single action. In fact, even when the two occurred close together in time, the questions of responsibility were different. The source side needed to confirm which object subsequent associations would adopt; termination needed to confirm whether shutdown advanced again.

This passage is not being kept in order to continue recommending it. When maintainers encounter the description of reuse by path, they need to know that it was an early working hypothesis. If it were simply deleted, the reasons the old changes affected only the storage location, and the reasons callers had early returns, would lose their provenance. The current position below does not overwrite this old text, but leaves a correction beside it.

## Correction: Separate Objects, Containers, and Entry Points

A later addendum separated "a new instance appears" from "the container can still provide objects." The earlier wording could easily put the two in one sentence, as if registering a new instance naturally meant that the container holding source could continue working. This inference was not retained. The instance handoff requires examining the old and new associations, while the container requires examining whether subsequent reads after replacement can still obtain objects; the two observations are related, but cannot substitute for each other.

The same addendum also narrowed the wording about old references. The old instance should not continue to be stored in new associations that adopt an instance, but this does not mean that all work already started must immediately switch to the new instance. The former is the storage boundary after replacement, while the latter is the read boundary for existing work. The current material does not provide a common switchover point, so the proposal cannot make that decision on behalf of specific callers.

The correction on the termination side did not declare "early return" entirely wrong either. It may be a local optimization at a particular call site, but cannot by itself prove that repeated requests are safe. If requests are to be handled at the entry point, it must at least be possible to observe whether the request arrives and whether shutdown advances again. Log fields, return text, and port behavior are not specified here.

Someone proposed drawing the source track and the termination track as a single state machine, because both involved a transition from having an object to having none. This proposal was not adopted. A unified diagram would erase two different handoff points and make "the old source was removed" and "shutdown did not advance again" look like the same kind of result. The proposal continues to retain two tracks.

## Adjacent Questions in the 2024 Addendum

If port reconnection also occurs near hot reload, the reconnection decision must not be forced into source replacement solely because the events are close in time. A separate document DOC-16 records the exception boundaries for termination capability and port reconnection. This page treats it only as an entry point for investigating an adjacent issue, without copying its handling approach.

One local question also remains unanswered: whether replacement completion and the container's continued provision of objects always occur at the same point. If they differ, the observed case should record them separately. "Replacement complete" must not obscure the container's state, nor can the import of `relative` be taken to mean that path normalization has already solved this problem.

This section does not add a new investigation procedure. It only marks the edges of the proposal: port reconnection, source map, breakpoint resolution, and switching all callers in sync do not automatically become decisions for this page merely because they appear in adjacent discussions.

## Review Excerpts and Unresolved Handoffs

The review excerpts retain two original remarks: "Overwriting is not cleanup." "A null target is not exempt from termination semantics." The first addresses the confusion between stored associations and old references, while the second addresses the confusion between caller returns and the termination entry point. They cannot replace test results, nor do they specify functions or log fields that the implementation must use.

There is still no common decision on whether work that has already obtained the old source during replacement should continue using the object it obtained then, or reread the new instance at a later stage. The former keeps the object stable for work that has already started, while the latter moves toward the new source sooner; the current material is insufficient to choose between them. Removing new stored associations must not be interpreted more broadly as immediately terminating all work that holds the old object.

The minimum trace that repeated termination needs to leave is likewise undecided. Recording only "the call reported no error" is too weak, while recording only the caller's return does not reveal entry-point behavior. The observation that can currently be pinned down is whether the shutdown action advances again. The exact output format is left for review of the actual entry point, rather than being invented here.

If a trial requires making the container unavailable before a new instance can be swapped in, or if old references can only be left to unrelated callers to guess at and clean up independently, the source track should stop. If a second request with a null target still advances a new shutdown action, the termination track should also stop. Stopping means that the current proposal has not brought the behavior under control, not that the old approach becomes recommended again.

## Current Position Added in Month 8 of 2025

When hot reload rediscovers the same compiled source, the old source instance must be replaced and old references removed; the release checklist item reads source container must remain available, and replacement must not make the container unavailable.

This position entered the record only in the latest revision. It separates the post-replacement requirements into three independently verifiable points: whether the newly discovered source becomes the instance used thereafter; whether the old source is no longer retained in new stored associations; and whether the container holding source can still serve subsequent reads after replacement. These three points cannot be used to prove one another on the basis of a single write to the storage location.

Here, "removing old references" concerns new associations and does not automatically require work that obtained the old source before replacement to reread. Whether that work continues to completion depends on the specific read path; if there is no material on that path, record only that it is unknown. The same path remains only a clue for tracing back and cannot reinstate the old approach's assumption of direct reuse.

A single successful registration is also no substitute for container availability. When tracing back, adoption of the new instance, removal of the old association, and whether subsequent reads can still obtain objects must be considered separately. If any one of these requires the container to become temporarily unavailable, this round of the proposal has not met the current position.

Null-target termination continues to be handled independently. Repeated requests must not advance the shutdown action one more time, but this page does not expand that requirement into a port reconnection strategy, nor does it require every caller to use the same kind of early return. What needs to be confirmed is whether the shutdown action advances again after the request passes through the entry point; the specific trace remains undecided.

## Trial Exit Criteria

When any of the following occurs, there is no point in continuing to add branches:

- The new instance can only be stored after the source container becomes unavailable;
- Old references require unrelated callers to guess at and clean them up independently;
- Repeated requests with a null target still trigger further shutdown advancement;
- Handling a null target requires deciding the full behavior of port reconnection at the same time.

The first two show that source adoption, removal of the old source, and the container's role in holding objects have not yet been separated. The third shows that repeated termination has not been placed at a point where it can be observed consistently. The last shows that an adjacent exception boundary has been pulled into this proposal. In these cases, preserve the objects from the observed case and the unknowns, rather than using a single "success" to obscure local failures.

"Add return points to all callers" is not adopted as an automatic remedy. It may save one call from going through shutdown once, but cannot establish whether the entry point knows the request arrived, nor guarantee that other callers do not handle null targets differently. "Have all readers immediately reread source" is not adopted either, unless a specific read path proves that the old object must be replaced immediately; the existing records do not establish that conclusion.

## Appendix: Old Examples

### Reuse by Path

The old example mapped compiled sources with the same path directly to an existing source, to illustrate that the change could be confined to the discovery point. This example is outdated. It did not record whether a new instance was created, nor did it record work that had obtained the old object before replacement. Paths are still useful for locating entry points, but cannot by themselves establish instance identity and removal of old references.

### Early Return for a Null Target

Another old example recommended that the caller return immediately upon seeing a null target. It avoided an apparent shutdown call, but left no observation of whether the termination entry point received the request. This example is no longer used to assess repeated termination, but only to explain why "the call did not continue" and "shutdown did not advance again" were later recorded separately.

### File Entry Point

When the source side needs to be traced back, still begin near `src/adapter/sources.ts`. First examine the stored associations when the compiled source is rediscovered, then examine adjacent paths that continue reading source after replacement. `l10n`, dependency injection, `xxHash32`, and `relative` provide only location clues and should not be elevated into lifecycle ownership.

This proposal addresses the adjacent questions of the handoff between old and new source instances, the container's continued provision of objects, and repeated termination with a null target. It does not present port reconnection, source map, breakpoint resolution, or switching all callers in sync as settled decisions. The two handoff questions remain in the body, awaiting material from specific entry points and read paths.

# Termination/Reconnection and File-Entry Troubleshooting Tree

Start with `src/adapter/debugAdapter.ts` and keep this as the entry point. Old troubleshooting notes point here from the issue name and call name, but they did not transcribe the full call relationships; the only thing directly visible is a few adjacency groups at the top of the file:

- `import * as l10n from '@vscode/l10n';`
- `import { Container } from 'inversify';`
- `import { Cdp } from '../cdp/api';`
- `import { DisposableList, IDisposable } from '../common/disposable';`

These items only indicate that the investigation starts near the adapter file. `Cdp` appears to lead toward the transport side, while `DisposableList` and `IDisposable` lead toward resource cleanup, but the call snippets left at the time were insufficient to determine which object is responsible for termination and which object is responsible for reconnecting.

The original recording convention was to capture the pre-call state first. If the port is still in use, first check whether the termination action returns; if the port is no longer there, do not immediately record that the process has ended. If the UI still shows the old connection, that still does not imply that the termination request was not sent. Here, "return" refers only to the call state that could be recorded at the time; it does not replace the target lifecycle record.

```text
Termination request
├─ Connection before call
│  ├─ Return ──> Record the return and port state
│  └─ No return ──> Stop at the call site
├─ No connection before call
│  ├─ Reconnect entry still appears to exist ──> Check the connection side
│  └─ No such indication ──> Preserve the port evidence
└─ Pre-call state missing ──> Do not fill in success or failure
```

At the time, the port and termination were put in the same tree to avoid looking only at the final page; this did not confirm that the two necessarily occurred in sync. When the connection recovers, first record whether recovery occurred before or after the termination returned; without these two records, do not treat recovery as evidence of termination success or failure.

`vscode-file authority` also appears in the same batch of notes. The old wording only said "look up the actual path along the directory structure"; it did not record the value of authority or the actual filename. The page-displayed URL, the directory hierarchy provided by the caller, and the local path are temporarily recorded separately; if any one is missing, stop at the path entry. # Troubleshooting Tree for Termination, Reconnection, and File Entry Points

This time we still start from `src/adapter/debugAdapter.ts`, but no longer present it as an index to the entire adapter. The old notes pointed to this file through issue names and call names; when tracing back, we need to locate the `v_prev` reference in `internal/JSD`. The direct neighbors visible in the file header are still `@vscode/l10n`, `inversify`, `../cdp/api`, and `../common/disposable`. These names can help us get back near the entry point, but cannot substitute for actual references.

## Old Tree Retained

The tree from 2023 grouped termination requests, port disconnection, and possible reconnection into a single branch. It originally only required checking the pre-call state first, to avoid inferring the process backward from the page's final frame:

```text
Before the call
├─ debug entry point already has a connection
│  ├─ Termination returns ──> Then record whether the connection is still usable
│  └─ Termination does not return ──> Preserve the call context, do not retry
├─ Port has no connection
│  ├─ Signs of a pending reconnection ──> Switch to the connection entry point
│  └─ No signs of a pending reconnection ──> Stop at the port state
└─ Neither side can be determined ──> Do not mark as successful
```

This tree was not deleted because it records the gap at the time: without the pre-call state, we cannot tell whether the port change came from termination, a pre-existing disconnection, or the page capture showing only the latter part. It also did not precisely define "signs of a pending reconnection". In the old notes, some people interpreted the port becoming available again as termination failure, while others interpreted the port being unavailable as termination having completed; both descriptions were merely guesses based on the final state.

## Separation After a Review

During the review, we first wrote down three separate questions: whether the termination request had returned, whether the target had ended, and whether the connection could still be re-established. All three can arise in a single observed case, but none can supply evidence for the other two.

If the termination action has returned and the connection is later established again, continue investigating the connection side first, and do not rewrite "connection restored" as "termination did not occur". Conversely, if the port temporarily disappears, we can only record that the connection side is not visible; without the handle state, do not describe this as the target having ended. The earlier wording that compressed all three into "port disconnected after termination" is no longer suitable for continued use, but is retained in the old tree to help explain where troubleshooting previously went off track.

The temporary branches used for the review are as follows:

```text
Termination request sent
├─ Return record exists
│  ├─ Port still visible ──> Check whether the connection object remains in the outer layer
│  ├─ Port temporarily not visible ──> Check whether a reconnection entry point exists
│  └─ Port state not recorded ──> Stop at the return record
└─ No return record
   ├─ Page shows the old target ──> Cannot substitute for a return record
   └─ Page does not show the target ──> Also cannot substitute for a return record
```

No reusable commands, complete output, or complete timeline for a single case were saved here. Thus, "check the connection object" is only a direction for tracing back, not proof that a particular fixed cleanup step exists; "check the reconnection entry point" also does not mean that reconnection will always occur after the port disconnects. When only the final page is available from the observed case, we should still return to the two items: the pre-call state and the termination return.

## The Separate File Path Thread

`vscode-file authority` is adjacent to the notes above because the two issues were mentioned in the same batch of troubleshooting, not because they have been confirmed to share an implementation. Early wording squeezed scheme, authority, and the local path into a single sentence, making them read like the same field. After the review, we first separated the objects: scheme is of type URL; authority is the host-like part of URL; the local absolute path is the path object that needs to be obtained to continue processing.

The old steps can still serve as the recording sequence:

1. Copy down the directory hierarchy provided by the caller.
2. Copy down the URL text seen on the page or in the request.
3. Record authority separately.
4. If a path object can be obtained, then compare it with the directory hierarchy.

Step 4 does not ask for the displayed URL to be used directly in place of the path. If no path object is available, stop at the URL record; if no directory hierarchy is available, do not fill in a local location based on authority either. This boundary is intended to prevent the notes from mistaking the appearance of a string for an actual file path.

`vscode-app` was noted in this round of discussion as an authority requiring special confirmation. At this point, all that is known is that it must not be mixed with the path part; whether it is involved in local absolute path resolution has not yet been settled on this page. Function names cannot be inferred from filenames, nor can responsibility for handling authority be inferred from `Cdp`, `Container`, or disposable-related import statements.

## Marginal Notes and Old Assumptions

An on-call marginal note left a reminder: first confirm whether it is the connection or the target that has disconnected. It had no call output attached, so it can only serve as a reminder from the time, not be expanded into a conclusion about the incident.

Another old assumption was "check reconnection first when the port is unavailable". This can serve as a starting point when connection records are available, but it does not cover cases where the port has disconnected while the target state is unknown, nor cases where the termination return has not yet been recorded. Here it is marked as a working assumption that needs revision and is no longer treated as the default path.

```text
Port temporarily unavailable
├─ Termination has already returned ──> Can continue investigating the connection side
├─ No termination return ──> Stop at the gap in call records
└─ No connection even before the call ──> Do not classify as a post-termination disconnection
```

There is a similar issue on the file entry point side: when URL and the directory structure appear together, the old notes tended to compare the text first; now we retain only the practice of "recording them separately" and cannot claim on this basis that the two will point to the same object.

## Observations Still Needed

Next, we need a record showing the following on the same screen: the pre-call connection state, the termination request's return, port changes, whether the connection was restored, and the target handle state when available. If any item is missing, stop at the corresponding branch rather than filling the gap with the final state shown on the page.

On the path side, we need a set of records that includes authority, the path part of URL, the caller's directory structure, and the local path object together. If only the text displayed on the page is available, this page can still only state that the text is insufficient to make a determination. The current version separates the old tree a little further, but does not present any unrecorded call edge as a fact.

# Troubleshooting Tree for Termination, Reconnection, and File Entry Points

This page was originally just a troubleshooting note near `debugAdapter.ts`. Later, the termination, port, connection recovery, and file path entry points all brought people back here, so the old tree, marginal notes, and later corrections were appended to the same page. They were not written in one pass as a unified procedure: the early section preserves what could be determined at the time, while only the later section contains the branches still in use today.

`src/adapter/debugAdapter.ts` is the starting point for tracing back. The only adjacent items directly visible in the file header are:

- `import * as l10n from '@vscode/l10n';`
- `import { Container } from 'inversify';`
- `import { Cdp } from '../cdp/api';`
- `import { DisposableList, IDisposable } from '../common/disposable';`

Old troubleshooting records point to this location using issue names and call names. `Cdp` allows tracing back to the transport side, `DisposableList` and `IDisposable` are reminders that there are objects to clean up here, and `Container` and l10n are other adjacent items visible in the same file. They do not establish a division of responsibility for termination, reconnection, or path resolution; the actual relationships still need to be checked individually in `internal/JSD`'s `v_prev` references.

## The Earliest Recorded Tree

The first entry in 2023 only required saving the pre-call state. The reason was simple: at the time, someone started by looking at the page's final frame, wrote "process ended" when the port disappeared, and wrote "termination failed" when the port reappeared. Both descriptions skipped over the termination request itself.

The original tree is shown below, with no retrospective changes to the wording:

```text
Termination request
├─ Connection present before the call
│  ├─ Return received ──> Record the return, then check the connection state
│  └─ No return ──> Stop at the call site
├─ No connection before the call
│  ├─ There still seems to be a reconnection entry point ──> Check the connection side
│  └─ No such indication ──> Preserve the port state as found
└─ Pre-call state missing ──> Do not mark as success or failure
```

The value of this tree is not that it was already correct, but that it preserved a stopping point: when the pre-call state is missing, the termination result cannot be filled in based on whether the page still shows the target or whether the port is temporarily available. The earliest note did not mention a connection factory, did not mention a process handle, and did not leave a complete call chain. It only recorded "return" and "port state" side by side.

At the time, "port unavailable" was also treated as a reason to look at the reconnection entry point first. This wording was later narrowed in scope, but do not delete it. It explains why later records repeatedly tied the connection lifecycle to the target lifecycle.

## Path Notes from the Same Batch

`vscode-file authority` was written in the margin during the same investigation round. The old notes did not say that it shared an implementation with termination; they only noted that the caller's directory structure and the URL shown on the page appeared at the same time, making it easy during a follow-up check to follow the displayed text all the way through.

The initial procedure had only three steps: first transcribe the directory hierarchy; then inspect URL; stop if no real path is found. Here, no sample of the "real path" was saved, so we cannot fill in a seemingly reasonable filename. The earlier section also did not distinguish scheme, authority, and the path component, so it cannot be treated as the current path description.

One erroneous tendency in the old notes was to treat the appearance of URL as a local file location. A later review found that this notation can conceal two gaps: the page text may not contain the caller's directory structure, and the directory structure may not have a corresponding path object. Without evidence from both sides, we can only know that a URL was seen, not where it ultimately ended up.

## On-Call Margin Addendum

A section of the on-call margin note lacked its full context and left only: "First confirm whether it is the connection or the target that broke." This sentence was retained because it pinpoints exactly the boundary missing from the old tree.

A broken connection concerns the port and connection-object side; the target ending concerns the termination-action and process side. They may occur one after another in the same incident, or only one of them may be recorded. If there is no return from the termination action, a port change must not be used to fill in the target state; if there is no connection-side record, the target ending must not be used to fill in whether the port can be re-established.

At the time, the margin also contained a more sweeping rule: "Check the port first; if that doesn't work, follow the reconnection path." This rule was not verified by field evidence as a universal sequence. When a connection record already exists, it can indicate the direction for follow-up, but it should not override scenarios in which there was no connection before the call to begin with, the termination request returned no response, or only the second half of the page was captured.

```text
The page only provides the final state
├─ Still displays the old target ──> Cannot infer that termination did not occur
├─ No longer displays the target ──> Cannot infer that termination has completed
├─ Port temporarily unavailable ──> Cannot infer that the target has ended
└─ Port later available ──> Cannot infer that termination failed
```

This is not asking anyone to ignore the page; it requires the page state to be interpreted alongside existing records. When the pre-call state is missing, retaining the page screenshot or text is enough; do not continue turning unknowns into a complete story.

## 2024 Year Review: Separating the Three Outcomes

After one review, the original statement "the port disconnects after termination" was split into three independent questions: whether the termination request has returned; whether the target has ended; whether the connection can be re-established. The page did not retain copyable commands or complete output, so here we can record only the order of checks, not fill in the actual observed result for each case.

The misclassification encountered during the review was this: the termination action returned, and the connection was later re-established, but the record described the restored connection as termination failure. The opposite misclassification was also seen: the port temporarily disappeared, and the record directly stated that the target had ended. Both classifications latched onto only one end state.

The new temporary tree becomes:

```text
Termination request sent
├─ Return recorded
│  ├─ Port still visible ──> Check whether the connection object is still retained by an outer layer
│  ├─ Port temporarily not visible ──> Check whether a connection recovery entry point appears
│  └─ Port not recorded ──> Stop at the return record
└─ No return recorded
   ├─ Page still shows the target ──> Does not substitute for a return record
   └─ Page does not show the target ──> Does not substitute for a return record either
```

Here, "retained by an outer layer" is not an assertion about a specific implementation. The disposable-related dependencies at the top of the file only indicate that resource objects may appear in or around this file; the shutdown order cannot be inferred from import alone. Similarly, `Cdp` is a transport adjacency, which is not enough to establish who initiates each step in port mode.

The revised recording convention separates observations into columns: one for the connection state before the call, one for the return from the termination request, one for port changes, and one for whether connection recovery appears afterward. When available, record the target handle state in a separate column as well. This is not meant to require complete observations in every case, but to make gaps visible; without handle state, do not record "returned" as "the process has ended".

## Deprecated default sequence

The following version was documented as the default path in the year 2024; it is now deprecated but remains on file:

```text
1. First confirm whether the port has disconnected.
2. If disconnected, prioritize finding a reconnection entry point.
3. If reconnection does not occur, then determine whether termination is complete.
4. If the page does not show the target in the end, record it as terminated.
```

Step 1 can serve as the starting point for connection-side observations; step 2 ignores the pre-call state and the termination return; step 3 leaves the termination determination too late; step 4 treats the display layer as a lifecycle record. This sequence is marked as deprecated here and should no longer be copied verbatim as incident-handling steps.

The old sequence was not simply deleted because it explains two types of legacy wording: one treats reconnection as evidence against termination, and the other treats port disconnection as meaning that the process handle has been released. Neither type reflects the current conclusions, but both still appear in old on-call records.

## The review criteria for authority have gradually become clearer

A similar separation was made on the path side as well. scheme indicates the URL type; authority is the host-like part of URL; the local absolute path is the path object used for further processing. Early on, all three were written on one line, making it impossible for readers to tell what a record actually stored.

Now, when reviewing the file entry point, first organize the existing material in the following order:

```text
Caller directory structure
        │
        ├─ URL text appearing in a page or request
        │       │
        │       └─ authority inside URL
        │
        └─ Path object obtained later
```

This is not a data-flow diagram, nor does it claim that the arrows represent function calls. It simply separates four kinds of records that are easy to conflate. The directory hierarchy can only show what structure the caller provided; displaying URL can only show what text was visible at the time; authority is only one part of URL; the local path object is what subsequent path handling actually needs to deal with.

If all you have is text displayed on the page, record the text and stop. If you have only the directory hierarchy, you still cannot fabricate a URL for it. If URL and the directory hierarchy are both present but the path object is missing, you still cannot conclude from string similarity that they refer to the same object. An old page once compared them this way, but that approach was later explicitly abandoned.

`vscode-app` is the authority that needs to be identified separately here. It must not be treated as a directory name, nor should it be joined with the path portion into a single string for comparison. Its path handling was left as pending confirmation in early documentation for a time; rules added later appear farther down this page and must not be back-applied to these earlier paragraphs.

## Constraints from the review

A review narrowed the scope of the page to "verify status from the entry point," rather than "assume implementation ownership as soon as a filename is seen." The review noted that `src/adapter/debugAdapter.ts` can be a verification entry point, but that does not mean it alone has termination capability, port reconnection, or authority parsing.

This feedback replaced several earlier shorthand formulations. The former "check termination as soon as this file is seen" was changed to: first confirm the entry point from that file, then follow actual references to see where the state appears. If the instance leaves no reference, leave the item unknown. `Container`, l10n, `Cdp`, `DisposableList` and `IDisposable` can help identify adjacent items, but they cannot be pieced together into a responsibility table.

The review also required the two lifecycles to be recorded separately:

```text
Target lifecycle: termination request, return, terminable handle state
Connection lifecycle: port state, connection recovery, reconnection entry point
```

They can affect each other during the same reproduction run, but a conclusion from one track cannot provide missing evidence for the other. Here, "terminable handle state" is also a recording slot; it does not mean that a handle can necessarily be obtained in every instance.

The original point of the review excerpt is very brief: "Don't label the break as a failure prematurely." No complete output was attached, so this page uses it only to constrain the recording order and does not turn it into an attribution for any particular anomaly.

## An incomplete reproduction attempt

A later attempt tried to record the pre-call state, the termination return, and connection recovery in the same round. The plan itself was clear: first establish whether a connection existed before the call, then trigger termination, then inspect the return, and afterward record the port and connection object separately. The material actually retained did not form a complete timeline, so this attempt cannot serve as comprehensive validation of the old tree.

It still yielded one useful correction: the termination return and connection recovery should be saved separately. When connection recovery appears, the observation point at which it appears needs to be retained; when there is no return record, recovery itself does not indicate whether the termination action completed. Likewise, a port not recovering does not indicate that the terminable handle has been released.

The reproduction did not provide a complete authority sample. The path issue remains at the level of "record URL, authority, the directory structure, and the local path separately". Having more records on the termination side does not justify also concluding that path resolution is performed through the same object.

## The troubleshooting branches currently in use

Later feedback called for including capability information and the startup results for port-mode in troubleshooting, but still branching based on the objects that can be obtained rather than guessing according to the old default order.

```text
Start up or recreate the scenario
├─ Capability information has not appeared
│  ├─ Only page state is available ──> Stop at the capability entry point
│  └─ Raw output is available but no probe is visible ──> Retain the raw output and recheck the entry point
├─ Browser port-mode has been reached
│  ├─ There are clues to connection recovery ──> Record the connection object and the termination side separately
│  ├─ There are no clues to connection recovery ──> Do not describe a port disconnection as an inability to reconnect
│  └─ Termination handle state is missing ──> Stop at the handle record
└─ Pre-call state is missing
   └─ Do not fill in the lifecycle from the final page
```

This tree retains three explicit stopping points. First, when capability information has not arrived, do not continue assessing termination support based on what remains in the UI. Second, when no connection-side information is visible in port-mode, do not infer the eventual ability to reconnect from a single port disconnection. Third, when the handle state has not been recorded, do not present the termination return and process exit as the same fact.

The old tree's "prioritize reconnection if the port is unavailable" is no longer the default action here. Only after the pre-call connection state and the termination return have been recorded separately is there a basis for investigating the connection side further. This adjustment corrects the old path; it does not mean that the reconnection entry point and termination are never related.

## Current requirements

The DebugAdapter capability must declare support for terminateDebuggee, and the capability probe label must remain debug adapter is available; the startup results for browser port-mode must also expose canReconnect, the connection factory for reconnection, and the terminable process handle.

This requirement adds detail about the specific relationship between capability declarations and launch results. When checking capabilities, retain the original probe text containing `debug adapter is available`; when checking browser port-mode, check separately whether `canReconnect`, a connection factory for reconnecting, and a process handle that supports termination are already present in the launch results. Do not summarize these three as "the port looks normal" again.

If the probe does not appear, stop at the capability entry point; if the probe appears but the text differs, retain the original text and do not record it as a successful match. If port-mode has started but `canReconnect` is missing, do not report it as non-reconnectable based on a temporary port disconnection, and do not fabricate a connection factory. If no state is available for a process handle that supports termination, the termination return value can only serve as a record on the termination side, and cannot replace a determination of whether the target has ended.

The current requirement does not make `src/adapter/debugAdapter.ts` the sole point of attribution. That path remains an entry point for tracing back; capabilities, launch results, and path objects must each be checked where they are actually referenced. The dependencies in the file header are still only for navigation.

## Current branches for file entry points

`vscode-file authority` remains on the same page as termination and reconnection, but it handles path entry points, not the target lifecycle. After obtaining URL, first identify the authority, then retrieve the path object separately. When the authority is `vscode-app`, the path must still be treated as a local absolute path; the `vscode-file` URL displayed on the page cannot replace this step.

```text
vscode-file URL
├─ authority = vscode-app
│  └─ Extract the path component, treat it as a local absolute path
├─ authority recorded, path object missing
│  └─ Stop at URL and the authority record
├─ Only page display text is available
│  └─ Save the text, wait for the caller's directory structure
└─ Directory structure, URL, and path object are all available
   └─ Compare them separately, do not treat any text directly as a local path
```

This branch is not used to prove support for terminateDebuggee, nor is it used to prove that the port has already recovered. It only prevents authority, the displayed URL, and the path object from being conflated into a single item. Only when the caller's directory structure, URL, and the local absolute path have all been retained is there material to continue comparing them; if any one of them is missing, stop at the corresponding point.

Early text compared authority and the path together first. That was the old way of recording information and is no longer applicable. This explanation is retained so readers can understand sentences in the old notes that did not separate the fields, not to encourage a return to the old approach.

## Related issues still open

There is still no complete record of the chronological order of the termination return, connection factory, and process handle in the same incident. The current requirements only call for them to be visible in their respective locations, not for this page to supply a fixed order. If the three sets of material from before, during, and after the call in the same reproduction become available later, add the chronological order then; until then, arranging the three into fixed steps along the deprecated tree would reintroduce the old misjudgment.

Another unresolved point is which layer the authority's path object is handed to after its processing is complete. The available material only supports checking the local absolute path in the `vscode-app` branch, and cannot be used to specify a function name, caller, or when resources are closed. Do not add symbol names based on the file path itself.

## Old appendix: Retained but not to be followed

There used to be a very short draft procedure at the bottom of the page:

```text
A. First check whether the port is disconnected.
B. After disconnection, prioritize handling it as a reconnection.
C. If termination has no separate state, judge based on the page's final state.
D. First compare authority and the path together.
```

A can continue to serve as a starting point for observing the connection side. B does not cover cases where the port is disconnected but the termination return is missing; C would treat the display layer as a lifecycle record; D would confuse the components of URL with the path object. B, C, and D have all been replaced by the stop conditions later on this page, and the old text is retained only to help identify historical records.

A reminder from a meeting also remains in the margin of the same page: do not label the disconnection as a failure yet, first confirm whether it is the connection or the target that has disconnected. It had no accompanying call output and did not form a complete exception record, so no further conclusions are drawn from it.

When reviewing this page, keep separate traces for termination issues along the target lifecycle and the connection lifecycle; for path issues, document authority, the displayed URL, the caller's directory structure, and the local absolute path separately. The old tree and old appendix remain to show how these entry points used to be mixed together.

# Wasm MIME and State Queue Decision

R26.9 First, handle this along two boundaries: the Wasm text source's MIME description is maintained by the side that produces the source, while serialization of the state queue is maintained by the caller.`src/cdp/api.d.ts` serves only as a reference point for the interface shape; no description of these two behaviors is added here.

Two placement options were compared at the time. One was to spell out MIME and the queue constraint next to Cdp's public types; the other was to keep `Api` generic, with the text source and queuing method determined only by the specific call path. The draft chose the latter. Visible in the file are generic declarations such as `Cdp`, `integer`, `Api`, and `AccessibilityApi`, and the file header imports only `IDisposable`; no object was seen that would be sufficient to bind the Wasm text source or queue ownership to the interface layer.

The state queue is tentatively treated as "call order is the serialization order." The close action is also tentatively treated as an ordinary operation at the end of the queue. No counterexample has been found for this judgment, but it is being retained as an implementation-side working convention for now.

Open questions: whether the text source's MIME needs a separate declaration on the editor side; whether the queue can still accept subsequent state changes during closing.

versions.body:
# Decision on Wasm MIME and the State Queue

This record has not been deleted because the two issues in R26.9 still bring readers back here: in what form the Wasm text source should be passed to the editor, and in what order state changes go out around shutdown. The initial draft compressed them into a single phrase, "handled by the caller," which did reduce changes at the interface layer at the time; only during a later review did it become clear that this compression also obscured two different issues.

First, retain the original meaning of the decision at the time: do not extend the generic `Api` for a particular Wasm text source, and do not add special rules for the state queue to `src/cdp/api.d.ts`. This decision concerned the interface surface, not a claim that ownership of the text source and queue was already clear. The old draft presented the latter half as a decision too, so this page was later often mistaken for complete implementation guidance.

The file itself was the starting point for the assessment at the time. At the beginning, it shows:

```ts
export namespace Cdp {
export type integer = number;
export interface Api {
```

The same file goes on to organize `AccessibilityApi`, `Accessibility`, `DisableParams`, and `DisableResult`. The file header contains `import { IDisposable } from '../common/disposable';`. These declarations present it as the central location for the structure of the Cdp protocol: namespaces, numeric aliases, interfaces, and parameter and result types are all laid out here. On this basis, the initial draft argued that putting a particular source format or a queuing process into a generic interface would make the interface carry concepts that not all calls share.

This trade-off was not unreasonable at the time. If neither the use sites of MIME nor the owner of the queue had been confirmed, adding fields, comments, or new interfaces directly around `Api` would instead turn guesses into public constraints. The initial draft chose to leave the interface unchanged. The problem came with the leap immediately afterward: because the type declarations contained no dedicated object, it was assumed that the caller would naturally handle describing the text source and serializing the queue. The first statement was a scope decision, while the second was only a working assumption.

## Three Formulations Considered at the Time

The first was to place both items near `Api`. This would allow readers searching the public types to see the explanations of text sources and state changes together, and make it easier to address the issues in one place. The cost was also clear: MIME does not necessarily belong to every Cdp call, and it is even less certain that the queue is a field or method of `Api`; without a suitable object, the comment would float above the interface, and readers would still not know where the actual relationship resides. The initial draft did not adopt this option.

The second was to leave everything to the respective call paths. The initial draft adopted this option and wrote it up as a single decision. MIME was treated as incidental display information attached after the text source was generated; the queue was treated as a natural consequence of the order in which calls were written. This required no changes to the generic declarations and no Wasm-specific names in the interface file. The cost was not documented at the time: the two paths would evolve separately, and readers could only follow the issue name back to a file that provided nothing more than an interface outline.

The third was to leave `Api` unchanged but add a narrowly scoped behavioral note near the interface, explicitly stating that the text source and queuing rules were handled by other objects. This approach was not rejected, merely deferred. The initial draft could not identify the objects that should be named and was concerned that a vague reminder would instead create another false entry point. So the note was not added.

The trade-off at the time can be summarized by the following state diagram. It describes how the old draft split the paths, not implementation relationships that were later confirmed.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Interface declaration lookup" as ApiReview
    state "Text source path" as SourcePath
    state "Caller queue" as CallerQueue
    state "Shutdown handling" as Closing

    [*] --> ApiReview
    ApiReview --> SourcePath: MIME checked separately
    ApiReview --> CallerQueue: Serialization checked separately
    CallerQueue --> Closing: Treated as the final operation in the initial draft
```

The part of the diagram most worth retaining is the starting point: `api.d.ts` is suitable for checking the interface surface, but its visible declarations provide neither a Wasm text source nor a queue instance. The old draft originally intended this to avoid incorrect interface design; later, however, it mistakenly turned "not seen here" into "does not need to be made explicit elsewhere."

## The Old Position on MIME

The initial draft treated MIME as display information attached after the text source was generated. In the account given at the time, the Cdp types only needed to give the caller an object it could continue processing, and the editor would then determine for itself whether it was Wasm text. This account did not specify the text source name or the URL format, nor did it explain at which boundary the MIME value was read. It was only one of the reasons for avoiding an extension to `Api`.

Therefore, "the side that produces the source maintains MIME" was not a conclusion about responsibility reached after a full check. At most, it expressed a design preference: not making a single source format part of a generic protocol interface. Extending that preference into "the editor does not need to explicitly identify the source" went beyond the type declarations visible at the time.

This is also why the old draft remains misleading. Wasm in the issue name brings people near `Cdp`, and `Api` is prominent enough in the file that it is easy to regard this as the sole location of the MIME contract. The actual review only showed that there was no dedicated definition here that could take the place of a description of the text source, and did not prove that MIME would not be used by the editor or a debugging client. The old draft provided neither a read site nor a source object to refer back to.

The entry point for follow-up checks is DBG-206. That card appeared later than the initial draft and cannot be used to prove that the initial draft already understood the specific relationships involving MIME; it can only explain why this old decision should no longer be treated as complete guidance. If Wasm MIME still needs to be examined, continue with that inspection target rather than drawing conclusions from the outline of `Api`.

## The Old Position on the Queue

The initial draft described the state queue in even less detail. The reasoning was: the caller first submits a state change and only then writes the next call, so call order is serial order; shutdown is just the last ordinary action. This account did not separately consider whether the state change had already entered the queue, whether shutdown changed the conditions under which the queue accepted new items, or whether callbacks after shutdown would still touch state.

The initial draft could not see the queue instance, state fields, or shutdown process, so it decided not to put queue rules into the Cdp types. This was a reasonable boundary within that scope. The mistake was in further interpreting "there is no queue in the type file" as "the order in which the caller writes calls is sufficient to guarantee queue serialization." The interface declarations provided no such guarantee, nor did they describe the order when shutdown and queuing meet.

The old draft recorded neither failure output nor a specific call sequence that could refute the assumption. All it retained was an oversimplified working convention: shutdown comes last, and subsequent state will not become a separate issue. That convention had brought the investigation to a halt outside the interface layer, without indicating whether the real focus should be the queuing boundary or the shutdown boundary.

DBG-222 later retained State Queue Serialization as a separate inspection item. This entry point should not be retroactively treated as a basis for the initial draft, but it is enough to show that the approach originally combined into a single sentence needs to be split apart. The question of whether the queue and shutdown affect each other can no longer be addressed simply by saying "the caller will write calls in order."

## Revised Position After Review

Only one part can still be retained: `Api` should not become a specialized interface solely because of a particular Wasm text source or a piece of state queue logic. This was a choice to limit interface growth, and it is consistent with the generic declarations visible in the file.

The parts that no longer apply must also remain here with the old draft: the order in which calls are written was treated as queue serialization, shutdown was treated as an ordinary final operation, and MIME was treated as incidental information that did not need to be consulted separately. They lacked sufficient support from the relationships between objects. The review did not replace them in this record with a new unified set of rules, but only separated the previously conflated judgments back into two lines of investigation.

For anyone still starting here, first confirm that `Cdp`, `integer`, `Api`, and `AccessibilityApi` form an interface outline; then examine Wasm MIME by following DBG-206, and examine State Queue Serialization by following DBG-222. DOC-20 records an adjacent interface review and should not replace these two lines of investigation.

# DWARF Disabling and Shutdown Ordering Proposal

This page originally set out to answer a narrow question: should the interface review for R26.9 treat DWARF Explicit Disable and Context Shutdown Order as a single change? The early notes placed both items alongside the bootloader's exit path. That wording remains because it explains why this proposal keeps being referenced; it does not prove that the two have the same caller, or that consolidating them at a single exit point would solve the problem.

## What Remains from the Early Draft

The initial material available at the time was `src/targets/node/bootloader.ts`. Direct dependencies at the top of the file included:

```ts
import { spawn, spawnSync } from 'child_process';
import * as fs from 'fs';
import * as inspector from 'inspector';
import match from 'micromatch';
```

These names are enough to show that the file touches process startup, file access, Inspector, and module matching. They do not directly establish the lifecycle of the DWARF toggle, nor can responsibility for context shutdown be assigned based on the file's location alone. The old draft treated "handle disabling first, then shut down the context" as a convenient order; there were no accompanying call examples, so that wording is retained as a working assumption from that time and should not be treated as the default interface for R26.9.

Only two kinds of practical differences were considered at the time. The first kept the boundaries separate: disabling DWARF would only change how symbol or source information is handled, while context shutdown would still follow the original termination action. The second used a shared exit: first let the runtime and Inspector states settle, then complete shutdown through a single exit, with that exit deciding whether to continue waiting. A shared exit leaves less to explain, but if any wait condition does not return, what was only an information-unavailability issue could become a session left open for a long time.

## Review Follow-up Notes

The subsequent review did not confirm the old ordering as definitive. DBG-207 records one `dependency_checked` action; this confirms that this line of investigation returned to dependency checks, but it does not endorse an interface choice. The search at another related entry point, DBG-223, used `context:false`, `context:true`, and `final:true`. These strings show that the review was indeed examining the relative placement of context flags and the final notification, but this page did not have enough call results to establish the order.

The candidate options therefore need to be compared on reversibility:

- **Separate boundaries**: Retain the explicit DWARF toggle and treat context shutdown as a separate action. The advantage is that existing callers do not have to understand both states at once; the disadvantage is that there may still be a window where one action has returned while the other is still waiting. If an experiment only shows a change in source information, that cannot be interpreted as shutdown having completed.
- **Shared exit**: Put the shutdown request, final notification, and required runtime waits on the same path. The advantage is that the order is easier to express through interface examples; the cost is that existing callers need to accept stronger wait semantics, and on abnormal exit it is harder to determine which step did not complete. Rollback must allow a return to separate boundaries, rather than just removing the new exit.
- **Delayed notification**: Leave the responsibility divisions in the first two options unchanged, and move only the final notification to after shutdown is confirmed. This is the most conservative option for callers, but if the confirmation condition itself depends on the context being shut down, it will end up waiting on itself. No examples yet show that this option can work on its own.

## Proposal Scope

This page favors trying separate boundaries first, then using interface examples to check the observed shutdown behavior, rather than switching to a shared exit first. "Try first" is not a finalized decision here: we need to see whether callers can distinguish four states—DWARF disabled, context still present, context shut down, and final notification. At a minimum, record each of the following: the flags passed in the call, whether the runtime returns, whether Inspector still holds the context, and whether the last notification carries a termination flag. Without these results, the ordering can only be described as unconfirmed.

One related issue is easy to conflate with this: disabling DWARF should not automatically remove source objects that are still discoverable by the debugger. The object name `WasmSource` appeared in the review notes, but this page does not have enough material to define its full lifecycle; if later examples are to cover WebAssembly sources, the point at which `WasmSource` is created needs to be checked separately before deciding whether it falls within this interface proposal. Do not use a "shutdown successful" log in place of observing whether source objects are still present or have disappeared.

## Rollback Conditions and Open Questions

If an experiment with a shared exit keeps existing callers waiting, or reports a case of missing DWARF information as a context shutdown failure, roll back to separate boundaries. If the final notification arrives before the context actually ends under separate boundaries, changing the log text alone is not sufficient; retain the failing input and call sequence, and compare the delayed-notification option again.

Three points remain undecided: who owns the last notification on abnormal exit; whether source information may still be requested after the disable toggle returns; and whether the shutdown action must be idempotent if it arrives more than once. The field name `closeCalls` is worth retaining in later interface examples, but this page has no results to show whether it counts requests or actual shutdowns. For follow-up review, start at `src/targets/node/bootloader.ts`, check the direct calls first, then return to the local material at DBG-207 and DBG-223; this navigation path does not mean ownership has already been determined.
