# Postmortem on Unmerged Records in the Quality Signal Dashboard

The Quality Signal Dashboard once entered a state that was hard to explain from the page's appearance alone: records for two revisions appeared simultaneously under the same "current revision" entry point. The two sets of content were not simply duplicates, and the result after path normalization also differed from the old record. After the entry point was restored, the page was accessible again, and the closing sequence was also restored; but these things did not happen at the same time, nor was enough material left to explain why the two revisions appeared side by side.

The preserved entry point for the incident state is `docs/adj-targets/incidents/targets-quality-signal-board-two-record-versions-not-merged.md`. It preserves the reading context in which the two revisions appeared side by side, rather than just a filename for convenient navigation. The old record was not deleted, and the other record was not rewritten as the sole version either. The changes in judgment seen in later reviews depended precisely on this difference remaining visible.

The challenge in this anomaly was not making the page accessible again, but distinguishing four things that are easily collapsed into a single statement: what the entry point displayed, how the index timestamps were ordered, whether the execution records captured the preceding steps, and which revision consumers treated as the current content. The first two can affect reading order, the third determines whether an execution record can be interpreted, and only the fourth concerns the scope of actual use. The available records do not connect them into a verifiable causal chain.

## Preserve the State First

The problem initially observed was narrow in scope. The content after path normalization differed from the old record, but both revisions were in the current entry point. There was no evidence of who wrote to the entry point, no evidence of which record was added first, and still less evidence that any consumer had already completed subsequent actions based on the old record. What can be confirmed here is that the records appeared side by side and differed; the write operation cannot be inferred from those differences.

So the first step was not cleanup, but preserving the original contents of `docs/adj-targets/incidents/targets-quality-signal-board-two-record-versions-not-merged.md` and stopping further retries that would overwrite the incident state. Further retries might have produced a tidier-looking page, but would have lost the state in which the two sets of content had appeared side by side. Keeping the original did not resolve the merge issue either; it only allowed later reviews to continue distinguishing "the two records seen at the time" from "the explanation added later".

The initial record also left several gaps:

- The exact time when the two revisions first shared the entry point;
- Which consumer actually read the old record;
- Whether the path-normalization differences contributed to the entry point remaining unmerged;
- Whether the same action placed both sets of content in the entry point.

These gaps were not a single, unified "cause to investigate". They concerned, respectively, the time of coexistence, the scope of use, path handling, and the source of the writes. The initial material was insufficient to identify any one of them as the cause.

## Recovery Came Before Cause Identification

The user path was later restored, and the closing sequence could also be restored. If the early notes said only "recovered", readers could easily take that to mean the issue had been resolved. On review, that statement needs to be understood within its original scope: recovery meant the access path could be used again, not that the relationships between the records had been fully sorted out.

Recovery left at least three questions unanswered: whether the old revision was still in the entry point, what the criteria for selecting the current record were, and whether any consumer had already read the old explanation. The page being accessible could only confirm that the access state had changed. It could not establish that the two revisions had been merged, nor that the old record had never had an effect.

Among the incident materials, there was once a retelling containing only screenshots. The screenshots can prove that the page displayed two pieces of content at a certain moment, but they lack the relationship between the two revisions, the entry version, and traceable context. The original input was later retained so that "path recovery" and "cause confirmation" could remain separate. The former already has observations; the latter still lacks material to close it out.

The fact that the closure order can be reconstructed also pertains only to the access process. It does not provide the ordering of the two revisions, the extent of the old explanation that was read, or complete the collection record. The closure order was included in the recovery record to prevent it from being omitted in retellings; it cannot be used to determine the relationship between the entries.

## Four Objects in the Entry

Describing the issue as "the current record is duplicated" would obscure the differences between the objects. The incident evidence distinguishes the following four categories of content:

| Object | Status in the entry | Scope that can be confirmed |
|---|---|---|
| Old revision record | Listed alongside another record | Still visible, not explicitly marked as historical content |
| Another revision record | Likewise a current candidate | Its position alone cannot establish that it overwrote the old record |
| Index time | Used to organize the entry content | Its relationship to the event and `targets-quality-signal` requires separate alignment |
| Execution record | Visible in partial materials | The corresponding collection record was not received |

The easiest simplification to make is "the record that appears later overwrote the record that appeared earlier." This statement assumes that index time is event time, that the execution record has a complete collection sequence leading up to it, and that the entry has already completed revision selection. None of these three assumptions is supported by the materials in this case.

Another simplification is to treat the two pieces of content as duplicate displays of the same revision. The path-normalized content differs from the old record, indicating that they differ at least in how they were presented at the scene. This difference is still insufficient to identify the write source, but it is sufficient to show that deduplication cannot precede the investigation. Deleting one directly would make it impossible to determine later whether the deleted item was the old content, the current content, or a candidate for which selection had never actually been completed.

"Current" in the entry can therefore only be interpreted as a display position, not automatically as a historical determination. It does not provide the time of entry, the adopting party, or the upstream collection sequence. The current entry is still worth retaining because it is the starting point for review; explanatory text that cannot be traced back should no longer occupy the explanatory slot.

## Reversal of the Index Timestamp

After DBGD-010, a follow-up recorded the observation that "the index timestamp and `targets-quality-signal` were reversed." Card actions require aligning the event, `targets-quality-signal`, and index time, while time differences that cannot be explained are to be recorded separately. This observation changed an earlier convenient assumption: content appearing later in the index does not necessarily represent an event that occurred later.

Index time is the field used to organize the entry. Event time describes when an anomaly or change occurred. `targets-quality-signal` is the object name for this quality signal. If the three are not aligned, one cannot use just one of these times to decide which revision should be marked current. The page order may be correct, and the event order may also be correct, but the two do not necessarily represent the same timeline.

This clue does not prove that timestamp inversion is the direct cause of two record versions appearing side by side. Its role is narrower and clearer: index order cannot replace the revision relationship, and an unexplained time difference cannot be erased as a single overwrite action. If the corresponding time points are recovered later, the event time and index time will still need to be compared separately; one field cannot replace the full temporal context.

During testing, DBGD-010 was handed over to someone who could modify the fixture. The reason for the handoff was that someone able to modify the fixture was needed to continue reproducing the issue. This addressed the operational requirements at the time; it was not a decision about the entry's long-term meaning. This is recorded to avoid mistaking personnel changes on the card for the technical action that caused the two versions to coexist.

At the index layer, only three conclusions currently remain:

1. The event, `targets-quality-signal`, and index time are retained separately;
2. Unexplained time differences continue to be listed separately;
3. Do not use index sorting to select a unique revision directly.

There are no stronger conclusions beyond this. In particular, timestamp inversion cannot directly establish which record should have prevailed, nor can it establish that the two revisions necessarily came from the same write path. The index clue can narrow the direction of further review, but it cannot replace the original entry artifact.

## Execution Records and Missing Collection Data

The records for DBGD-012 brought the issue to another layer. The public statement left after the risk check was: the collection record corresponding to the execution record never arrived at all. It was subsequently clarified that missing collection should be marked as unknown, and the execution record should no longer be filled in as zero.

Here, unknown means that no collection data was obtained, not that a value of zero has already been observed. Zero means that collection was completed and produced an empty result; unknown means that this part of the pipeline provided no record that could be traced back. Both may appear as "no value" at the entry point, but they are completely different when interpreting the two revisions. Treating unknown as zero will make readers mistakenly think that a complete empty result exists, and they may therefore interpret one version of the record as having no changes.

A screenshot cannot fill in a collection record that never arrived. The execution record also cannot, by itself, stand in for the collection step that came before it. Even if the execution record and a revision appear on the page at the same time, that cannot confirm that the revision has complete input context, much less allow it to automatically merge the two records.

DBGD-012 was handed over to a colleague on the same team because the original owner was on leave. This was continuity of the handling process, not a technical explanation for the missing collection. Later, the entry retained the navigation for "current revision" and removed explanatory text that could not be traced back. This adjustment did not remove the gap itself, nor did it fill the collection gap with a passage that merely appeared complete.

At the execution-record level, what can be confirmed in this case is:
| May be retained | Must not be added |
|---|---|
| The corresponding collection record did not arrive | The collected values for this segment were zero |
| This segment is treated as unknown | A revision had no preceding changes |
| The unsourced explanation has been removed | The cause of the missing collected data has been found |
| The navigation entry still exists | The two versions of the record have been automatically merged by the execution records |

This comparison addresses only the missing collected data in this incident and does not define broader state meanings for the Quality Signal Dashboard. Its practical purpose is to prevent "no record" from being rewritten as "the recorded result is zero".

Missing collected data and index inversion cannot explain each other either. The former indicates that a segment of data did not arrive, while the latter indicates that several temporal objects need to be realigned. The current materials still cannot establish whether the gap occurred before, during, or after the entries appeared side by side. The presence of execution records on the page is also insufficient to fill the gap in this period.

## Two explanations that were once viable but later became invalid

At least two convenient explanations remain in the old materials. The first account was: path normalization differed, so the two revisions were merely two displays of the same content. Path differences were indeed the earliest observed phenomenon, but they can only prove that the displayed results differed, not that the normalization process wrote the two revisions into the same entry, nor that it would automatically select the current version. This account is therefore retained as an early observation, but no longer as a cause.

The second account was: since the entry contains execution records, treat empty collected data as zero, then use that to explain the absence of changes between the two versions. It was later confirmed that the collection records had never arrived, overturning this premise. Missing collected data is not empty collected data, and execution records cannot supply a nonexistent predecessor in its place. The entry no longer uses zero to smooth over this gap.

Another overgeneralization is easy to make after recovery: the user path has been restored, so the old entry had no actual impact. This judgment generalizes from one successful access to all adopters being unaffected. The available materials contain neither the scope of adoption nor records of specific users reading the old explanation, so they can only confirm recovery of the observed path, not that all reads were without consequences.

These old accounts have not been erased from the historical materials. They show how understanding changed: first treating path differences as a possible cause, then mistaking execution records for complete input, and finally narrowing the judgments separately using the index and collection materials. When retaining these accounts, the reasons they could no longer be used later must also be retained.

The second account also confused "no value" with "a value of zero". If it were written back into the old records, later readers would see an apparently complete empty result, but would not see that the collected-data segment had in fact never arrived. The revision therefore does not replace the old account with a polished new sentence, but leaves the old judgment where it appeared and marks in later records the failed premise that made it invalid.

## The actual scope of the actions taken

Handling the entry did not select one revision as the permanent winner. Three actions remain in place: keep navigation to the "current revision"; remove explanatory text that cannot be traced back to a source; mark segments whose collection records did not arrive as unknown. When index time differs from event time, neither is used to overwrite the other.

These actions address the risk of misreading the entry, not the cause of the incident as a whole. They let readers see that the navigation remains, the unsourced explanation has been taken down, and missing collected data has not been recorded as zero, as well as that the two old records have not been reworked to masquerade as a single seamless history. They do not answer when the two versions first appeared side by side, nor which adopters had already used the old explanation.

DBGD-005 left the quality signal dashboard's owner slot unfilled. The temporary assignee only handles actions that are due and does not write a long-term interpretation for the quality signal dashboard. This boundary is closely connected to this case: when no one is clearly assigned to own the long-term interpretation, someone is especially likely to add an explanation of the "current revision" that cannot be verified against its source, just to make the handoff easier. The approach taken here did not turn temporary actions into a long-term interpretation.

The cards also remain limited in scope. DBGD-010 provide an entry point for index time alignment, DBGD-012 provide an entry point for missing collection data and explanations without sources, and DBGD-005 provide an entry point for the unfilled owner slot. They address time, supporting material, and long-term interpretation respectively, and cannot substitute for one another. DOC-45 only record the impact after these issues appeared together in a single entry point anomaly.

Changes in responsibility on the cards cannot be treated as a technical timeline. The transfer of DBGD-010 to someone who could modify the fixtures indicates the operational conditions needed during reproduction; the transfer of DBGD-012 due to leave indicates that handling did not stop with the original owner; the unfilled owner slot for DBGD-005 indicates that the long-term interpretation had no fixed owner. None of the three provides evidence of writes to the two revisions.

This entry point cleanup therefore had a clear stopping point: retain the navigation, remove explanations that could not be verified against their sources, preserve the side-by-side state, and mark missing collection data as unknown. It did not go on to consolidate the surrounding objects into a unified state, nor did it use the temporary assignee to fill in a long-term interpretation. This left unresolved items, but did not package the unknown as a definite answer.

## Impact Window

The known impact is concentrated on the entry point's explanatory capability. When two revisions appear together under "current revision", readers may mistake old content for a new explanation, or mistake index position for the chronological order of events. When collection records have not arrived but are entered as zero, readers may also interpret missing material as a revision having no changes.

There is currently no material proving that all quality signals were affected, nor is there material proving that every adopter read the old entry point. For scenarios where the revision can be confirmed elsewhere, this does not establish that the result must be wrong; for scenarios that can only rely on this entry point, the scope of adoption has still not been determined. The impact assessment therefore stops at a narrower conclusion: people relying on this entry point for interpretation cannot reliably determine the temporal context and data status corresponding to each of the two sets of content.

The recovery window likewise cannot substitute for the impact window. Restoring the access path shows only that a particular path later became usable; it provides no record of who read the old entry, how long they read it, or which explanation was adopted. Without that evidence, we do not generalize recovery into full recovery, nor write the unknown adoption scope as zero.

The impact is not "all pages were wrong." The current evidence supports only that the entry simultaneously displayed two revisions, and that path-normalization differences, an index-timing issue, and missing collection data existed. There is no record of whether a particular consumer viewed the old content or adopted it afterward. Limiting the impact to unreliable interpretation preserves the observations already made without overstepping the gap in the adoption scope.

Recovery actions and impact assessments need to be kept separately. The user path being available again and the closure order being recoverable show that the access side changed; they do not answer whether the two revisions at the entry are still distinguishable, whether the preceding collection steps have been completed, or whether the adopting party changed. A green page can represent only access status; it cannot represent these relationships.

## Timeline Ordered by Changes in Understanding

The sequence below records how the assessment changed; it does not treat every action as a cause:

| Stage | What was visible at the time | Action taken at the time | Understanding retained later |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial discovery | Two revisions shared the current entry, and the path-normalization result differed from the old record | Saved the original input and stopped further overwriting | The live state showed parallel revisions, but the cause was unknown |
| Path recovery | The user path and closure order could be recovered | Did not use the green result to overwrite the prior state | Access status was restored; that does not mean merging was complete |
| Index review | The event, `targets-quality-signal`, and index time needed to be aligned | Listed unexplained time differences separately | Index order cannot substitute for event order |
| Test handling | DBGD-010 was handed to someone who could modify the fixture | Continued working through the reproduction conditions | A personnel handoff is not a technical cause |
| After the risk check | The collection record corresponding to the execution record had not arrived | Retained the missing value and recorded it as unknown | A missing value cannot be written as zero |
| During entry cleanup | An explanation for the current revision existed but could not be traced back | Removed the explanation and retained the navigation | The navigation remained usable; the basis was not fabricated |
| Current review | Coexistence, time differences, and missing collection remain separate layers | Did not force them into a single cause | The adoption scope and the time of first coexistence remain unknown |

At initial discovery, there was no conclusion of "missing collection"; that conclusion came from later evidence. The reversed index order also did not automatically explain the collection issue; it only constrained how the entry could be organized by time. Only by placing these assessments back into the stages where they emerged can we see why the earlier material did not support the current framing from the outset.

In the timeline, "current" refers to the wording in the live record, not a single conclusion added later. The early stage showed only page coexistence and content differences; the path-recovery stage added access status; only at the index-review stage did misaligned time objects appear; only after the risk check was it confirmed that the collection data had not arrived. The assessments from the latter two stages must not be back-projected into the initial discovery.

## Cleanup Methods Not Used

Some might be inclined to move the old revision straight to the history section, pin the other as current, and leave the missing collection data blank. This would make the entry point tidier, but would hide the fact that the two revisions once appeared at the same time, and would also leave readers unable to tell whether "no collection data" means that material is missing or that the page has chosen not to display it.

This case did not use this kind of one-off cleanup. Keeping the old record does not mean the old explanation is still correct; removing the unsourced explanation also does not mean the entry point now has a complete account of the cause. Differences in path normalization were retained as an initial observation and cannot be elevated to an attribution of technical cause; the claim that it should be treated as zero was dropped after it was confirmed that the collected data had not arrived; the claim that recovery means completion does not hold because the scope of adoption is unspecified.

The purpose of preserving history is to let later readers see where judgments were overturned, not to require them to keep following the old practices. The current entry point's availability, the relationship between revisions, the indexing time, and the collection status still need to be read separately. Any cleanup that leaves only the final green page will lose the most valuable details of how this anomaly changed over time.

The narrower approach of "keeping only the revision that appeared last" was not used either. The available material does not provide enough information about entry times, nor does it state that indexing time is equivalent to event time. Deleting the old record would make it impossible to recheck the scope of adoption and the original differences; leaving the missing collection data blank would make the blank look like a normal zero result. Both kinds of cleanup alter the meaning of the state as found.

## Unresolved Items

1. Recover the exact time when the two revisions first appeared in the same entry point. The current material only establishes that they once coexisted and does not provide sources sufficient to determine their order.
2. Align the event time, `targets-quality-signal` and indexing time. Continue to list unexplained time differences separately, without choosing one field to overwrite the others.
3. Check whether the collection records failed to arrive before, during, or after the period when the revisions coexisted at the entry point. The available material only confirms that they did not arrive and cannot establish when the gap began.
4. Verify the scope of adoption of the old explanation for the entry point. Without a scope of adoption, do not take recovery of the user path to mean recovery for all consumers.
5. Clarify how the two revisions should represent the relationship between historical and current states. A temporary takeover cannot stand in for answering this question, nor can it be resolved by adding an unsourced explanation.
6. Confirm whether both pieces of content came from the same write operation. There are currently not enough records to attribute the side-by-side state to a particular writer or a single path.

These items correspond to the gaps left by this case, not a request to redo the peripheral projects as well. They concern, respectively, the time of coexistence, time alignment, where collection data was missing, the scope of adoption, the form of representation, and the source of the writes. Each item requires its own supporting material, and none can make up for another through page recovery or card handoffs.

The unresolved items also cannot be arbitrarily linked together. If the time of coexistence is found first, whether consumers have read the content still needs to be checked separately; if the indexing time is aligned, that still cannot be used to fill in the collection records; if the collection records are later recovered, that still does not automatically establish whether the other revision was adopted. Each gap has its own source of evidence, and the current page only preserves their relationships and limitations.

The owner vacancy for DBGD-005 was not filled with a long-term owner during this incident either. The temporary assignee only needs to handle actions as they come due, and must not write up a set of interpretations for the Quality Signal Dashboard that have not been checked against the records just because a handover is needed. This unresolved status is part of the maintenance arrangements and is recorded separately from the technical relationship between the two versions of the content.

## Review entry points

DBGD-010 retain an entry point for aligning the index timestamp with `targets-quality-signal`; DBGD-012 retain the fact that the unsourced "current revision" explanation has been removed, along with the determination that missing collection data is treated as unknown; DBGD-005 retain the owner vacancy for the Quality Signal Dashboard and the scope of the temporary assignment. The three cards provide three local entry points, not a confirmed causal chain.

The handling outcomes currently retained on this page are: the side-by-side state of the two revisions remains available for review; the navigation entry point still exists; explanatory text that cannot be checked against the records has been removed; collection records that have not arrived are no longer filled in as zero; the unexplained time offset between the index and the event is still retained. The fact that the user path and closure order can be reconstructed is also retained, but is no longer used to imply that the relationship between the records has been resolved.

Still unconfirmed are when the two revisions first appeared side by side, whether the index inversion contributed to their not being merged, which adopters used the old entry point, and where along the timeline the collection gaps occurred. Without these materials, "current revision" cannot be presented as the sole and complete conclusion.

When reviewing, first check the side-by-side state at the original entry point, then check the index timestamp and collection records separately. The entry-point file is where the state of this case is preserved, and does not provide explanations on behalf of the cards that go beyond their local records. The cards can point to time alignment, missing collection data, and the owner vacancy, but cannot piece the three issues together into an already confirmed story.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as Consumer
    participant P as Quality Signal Dashboard Entry Point
    participant E as State Records
    participant I as Index
    U->>P: Read the current revision entry point
    P->>E: Preserve the side-by-side state of the two revisions
    P->>I: Display the index time
    I-->>E: Event time and index time must be compared separately
    E-->>U: The path can be reconstructed, the scope of adoption is still unknown
```

This diagram only shows the reading order among the objects in the preserved state. It does not mean that the index has already selected a revision, nor that the execution records already include the full collection history leading up to them. The two records, the index time, and the collection status must still be reviewed separately.

What remained at the end of this case was not a neat single state, but a set of partial facts that can be rechecked: the entry point had displayed two revisions simultaneously; the path normalization result differed from the old record; the access path and shutdown order were later restored; the events, `targets-quality-signal`, and indexing times need to be aligned; the collection record corresponding to the execution record did not arrive; missing segments are treated as unknown; explanatory text that could not be verified was removed; the scope of adoption of the old entry point and the start time of parallel use remain unknown. Any further attribution requires the corresponding original material to be supplied.

# Entry point migration index for package integration collaboration

This index captures the state from when ui-package-integration switched from the old entry point to the current one. It covers cross-package dependencies, version combinations, and consumer integrations around ui; seeing a new entry point in the directory doesn't mean the migration is complete. Compatibility callers may still be using the old entry point, and version combinations can't be assessed by looking only at the latest set.

Two approaches were compared at the time: continuing through `cache identity`, or splitting out the `remote source`. Both names are retained because they have different failure exit points. Tracing the issue back through cache identity stops near the original entry point; after the remote source is split out, callers need to confirm that they're reading the new object, not just check whether a new location appears in the directory. The eventual preference was for the latter, but this page did not turn it into a new unified rule, and some of the guidance is now outdated.

Record the migration in the following order:

1. First, find the old and current paths in the index and record the corresponding version combinations.
2. Choose a consumer that's still in use and read through to the current entry point from its original call site; seeing only a new directory entry doesn't count as a pass.
3. List compatibility callers still using the old path separately. Don't collapse different batches into a single final status; in particular, preserve the differences seen on the first read.
4. If the result from the current entry point is inconsistent with the consumer's, pause at that caller first, retain the old path and the recorded state, then decide whether to restore it.

When restoring the old path, first move the affected callers back to the old entry point, then undo the version-combination switch for this batch; don't clear the old entry point records at the same time. The active callers of `rollback endpoint` were not verified at the time, so the restore operation cannot be described here as a validated full rollback. After restoring, you still need to use the same real consumer to confirm that the old entry point is readable; directory state is only a supporting clue.

The index file is at `docs/adj-ui/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md`, and adj-ui still maintains the body and attachments. Side paths with similar names are not automatically included; guidance that can't be traced back through this file is retained as an outdated record. If someone taking over later adds results, they should add them directly to the relevant migration batch, old path, or current path, not overwrite intermediate caller details with a single final status.

# Team Shared Entry Point Maintenance FAQ

Recording the three questions that kept coming up at the time, so we don't have to start the search over at the shared entry point every time.

**What can the existing source-identity entry point prove?**
If the candidate path can be found through the entry point and is grouped under the same source identity, downstream can initially proceed as though the cumulative chain already covers the target behavior.

**Who withdraws the candidate path?**
By default, the person who proposed the path withdraws it. The entry point maintainer only checks whether any candidates are still listed there.

**Under what conditions can it be closed?**
Once the candidate is withdrawn and the entry point hasn't changed, it can be closed first; if regression testing is completed a little later, that shouldn't block cleanup either. This judgment is not yet supported by original execution records.

# Team Shared Entry Point Maintenance FAQ

The shared entry point was once used as a quick confirmation point: if a path could be found and the candidate disappeared from the list, some people considered the work done. This FAQ retains that guidance because old links still bring people here; the earlier answers to the first and second questions should not be used directly to plan cleanup or card closure.

## What can the existing source-identity entry point prove?

The earlier answer was: if the candidate path was grouped under the same source identity and could still be found through the shared entry point, the cumulative chain was considered to have covered the target behavior. That judgment was later overturned by feedback from the field. The entry point only shows that paths have a common lookup location; it cannot prove that the cumulative chain actually achieves the target, or that the existing regression tests have passed.

Recording the entry point's status as "covered" makes it particularly easy to miss two things: whether the path is only being retained temporarily, and whether it is still possible to return to the original endpoint after cleanup. The former is partly visible in the entry point; the latter isn't. The old answer is kept here to explain why some people at the time ended their checks after looking only at the source identity.

## Who is responsible for withdrawing candidate paths?

The old draft assigned withdrawal to the person who proposed the path, while the entry point maintainer was only responsible for checking whether the candidate was still there. That division assumed the proposer controlled both the cleanup and rollback actions; the actual records did not establish that link.

Therefore, without original execution records, do not infer who withdrew the path from the entry point, the candidate path, or a particular list change. The question can be logged, with the answer left unknown. Don't rewrite "the candidate has disappeared" as a claim that a specific person completed cleanup; those are not the same thing.

## Under what conditions can it be closed?

The old quick answer was "Once the candidate is withdrawn and the entry point is unchanged, it can be closed first, with regression testing completed afterward." That answer remains in the historical context above, but is no longer suitable as a basis for closure. The rule the team continues to use is: a card can only be closed when the cumulative chain's target behavior and the existing regression tests both pass, and there is evidence for the cleanup and rollback paths.

DOC-50 contains notes on single-variable reruns; these can help revisit an attempt, but cannot on their own replace records for the cumulative chain, cleanup, or rollback.

This page does not provide the missing answer about who withdrew the path. The old page still misleads people precisely because it once presented entry point lookup, the candidate's disappearance, and permission to close as a very short chain.

When adding records, append only evidence that can be traced back to the original execution: if any one of the card number, run time, or rollback endpoint is missing, keep the answer unknown. Don't use the entry point maintainer's day-to-day responsibilities as a substitute for confirming who withdrew the path.

# Decision Record: Maintaining the Team's Shared Entry Point

This discussion focused on Lanqiao Developer Tools's shared team entry point. After tracing back through `src/adapter/sources.ts` and source-related calls, we recorded an initial working hypothesis: the entry-point differences might be due to changes to the source-identity window, not necessarily a replacement of the entry point itself. At the time, this assessment still needed to be verified in practice.

The meeting compared two options: keep the existing source-identity entry point, or adjust the window. The decision was to keep the existing entry point for now and leave window adjustments out of this round. This lets the team continue to look up shared materials via the existing path without recording unconfirmed compatibility costs as already addressed.

The old entry point is retained as a path that can be withdrawn. At this stage, the recorded impact is on collaboration: changing the entry point will change where people start looking for shared materials. # Decision record for maintaining the team's shared entry point

This round, the shared entry point for Lanqiao Developer Tools's team was not handled on the premise that "switching to another window will solve it". The discussion had a narrow focus: whether team members, after obtaining the shared materials, should continue tracing back through the current source-identity entry point or first adjust the window to which the entry point applies. The former preserves the starting point for finding materials, while the latter brings the entry point's scope, the interpretation of old materials, and compatibility into this round together. This is a discussion of a maintenance decision, not a redefinition of permanent ownership for `src/adapter/sources.ts`.

## Start from the file location, but do not treat the location as the conclusion

The initial draft traced back through `src/adapter/sources.ts` and source-related call names, leaving a working hypothesis: differences in the entry point might come from a change to the source-identity window, rather than the entry point having been replaced. File locations and call names are enough to show where the investigation started at the time, but they cannot establish the entry point's organizational ownership on their own, nor can they prove that a window change has already occurred.

The initial draft therefore left this judgment pending review rather than presenting it as the root cause of a failure. It also did not assume that all users reached the shared materials in the same way. Being able to find the entry point and still being able to interpret old materials in the original way after the entry point's scope expands are two different things.

The review confirmed only the following: the current entry point can still serve as the starting point for finding the team's shared materials. This round had no materials proving that all existing usage patterns would remain compatible after a window adjustment, nor any materials supporting an expansion of this maintenance work into changes to runtime, performance, or caller behavior. This distinction is retained because "the entry point is still there" answers only the location question, not the compatibility question raised by a window change.

## The two approaches compared

### Retain the current source-identity entry point

This option continues to use the existing entry point. When looking for shared materials, the team does not have to change both the starting point and the basis for interpretation at the same time; subsequent reviews can also follow the same local path back to the original target. For this round, its decisive advantage is that the scope of impact is visible, allowing observed entry-point behavior to be separated from unconfirmed window issues.

The trade-off is that questions arising from the window boundaries will not disappear automatically. Anyone who needs a broader scope of applicability must still describe that scope change separately, rather than treating the current entry point's accessibility as proof of compatibility after expansion. Retaining the current entry point also does not mean it has gained new capabilities, only that this round will not layer unreviewed changes onto it.

### Adjust the entry-point window

The argument for adjusting the window is that it might better fit new ways of collaborating and reduce some questions about where the entry point applies. But this is not just a change of location: old materials would need to be reinterpreted, users who depend on the current entry point might need to change as well, and any incompatibility would require confirmation that the original way of finding materials could be restored.

The meeting did not treat "it might be more convenient" as grounds for approval. The existing materials did not cover the combination of a window adjustment with old materials, existing usage patterns, and rollback paths, nor were there actual results showing which scopes would remain valid after the adjustment. This option therefore remains in the comparison record but was not adopted in this round's decision. The objection was not that adjusting the window could never have value, but that this round could not contain the compatibility costs within a localized, reviewable scope.

## Decision and scope

This round retains the current source-identity entry point without adjusting the window. Approval extends only as far as frozen code, reproducible logs, or public protocol boundaries can support. Frozen code serves here as review material, not an organizational responsibility matrix; reproducible logs that cannot lead back to the same entry point also cannot be used to prove window compatibility; public protocol boundaries can support only the behavior they explicitly cover.

What this decision actually resolves is "where the team starts looking for shared materials". It does not resolve how all usage patterns should migrate after the window expands, nor does it make unverified compatibility true by default. If subsequent evidence covers only a single window or a single usage pattern, the decision extends only to that specific area, rather than being casually rewritten as a comprehensive rule for the team's shared entry point.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Team shared materials] --> B[Current source-identity entry point]
    B --> C[Review along the existing path]
    D[Adjust the window] --> E[Reconfirm compatibility]
    E --> F[Old entry point: available for rollback]
    B --> F
```

The diagram preserves the relationships actually compared in this round: the current entry point continues to serve as the starting point for finding materials, a window adjustment requires separate confirmation of compatibility, and the old entry point does not disappear from the record or the actual lookup path. It does not depict unconfirmed window outcomes as successful, nor does it depict file location as team ownership.

## The old entry point and rollback boundaries

The old entry point is retained as a rollback path. It is not retained to create a second set of shared entry points, but to let the team return to the original way of finding materials if a future window adjustment is rejected or an incompatibility actually occurs. The old entry point cannot remain merely a verbal "backup plan"; it must remain in the materials as a target to which this round's decision can roll back.

The rollback boundaries are therefore fairly specific. If an adjustment is made later, rollback means reverting the window or entry-point change, not writing new conclusions back into old materials. If a review proves only a particular entry-point behavior, update only the corresponding part; if it confirms only how collaboration is routed, the record should stop at that routing; if there is still no evidence of compatibility, the old entry point remains the rollback endpoint. A single reply or screenshot can help locate a problem, but cannot replace a complete entry-point review.

Retaining the old entry point does not mean it covers scopes that have not yet been checked. Nor does it mean that all historical materials will automatically acquire a new interpretation. The next maintenance round must first identify whether the actual change is to the entry point, the window, or the materials themselves; when the three are mixed together, it is impossible to tell which layer a rollback actually restores.

## Practical impact and collaboration routing

For team members, the immediate impact is that the starting point for finding shared materials remains unchanged for now. If the question is simply "where to find the materials", start with the current entry point. If the question requires proof of compatibility after the window expands, it cannot be approved simply because the entry point is still accessible; such questions must record usage patterns and entry-point scope separately.

As the integration-side contact, Yuan Jing is responsible for bringing feedback involving old links or screenshots back into the entry-point discussion. Materials she can verify from the integration side can explain where the feedback came from, but she cannot claim from memory alone that the window change has been completed; when follow-up is needed, the old links or screenshots should be revisited. This routing preserves the entry-point behavior seen from the integration side without expanding it into a judgment about internal JSD code.

Thomas Qian is responsible for checking the local entry-point materials and retaining counterexamples, a diff, or replies from the owner as evidence for reviewing the decision. The purpose of counterexamples here is to test whether the working hypothesis still holds, not to provide advance proof in favor of the window-adjustment option. If a new diff touches only a local part of the entry point, update only that part of the record; if an owner reply only explains who receives feedback, do not interpret it as a compatibility conclusion either.

Feng Yue does not own the local JSD entry point. When input is needed on the runtime observation side, accept only code snippets or results that she can verify from adjacent materials. Her input can help distinguish an observation about an entry point from a runtime result, but cannot replace a review of the local entry point. This arrangement routes collaboration; it is not a new declaration of which team `src/adapter/sources.ts` belongs to.

## Reasons it was not adopted at the time

Adjusting the window was not proven to be the wrong option. It was not adopted because the materials that could be checked in this round were sufficient only to support retaining the current entry point, not to cover all of the following changes at once: how old materials would continue to be interpreted, whether users who depend on the current entry point would treat a path change as a change to the target, and whether the original entry point could be restored after a failed adjustment without rewriting historical materials. Packaging these issues as a single instance of "completed entry-point maintenance" would make the decision appear broader than the evidence.

Likewise, the current entry point is not guaranteed to be correct without qualification. Retaining it merely avoids introducing a second point of change when evidence is insufficient. If entry-point behavior is later found to have actually changed, it is still necessary to distinguish first whether the change is to the source-identity window, the entry-point location, or the shared materials themselves; the fact that this decision chose to retain the entry point must not be used to force later observations to fit the judgment made at the time.

## Checks left for future revisions

This version adds the distinction established after an actual review: the entry point can be retained as the starting point for finding materials, while compatibility after window expansion remains unconfirmed. Accordingly, the option not adopted, the objections to it, and the rollback boundaries for the old entry point all remain in the decision rather than being compressed into a single sentence saying "no adjustment for now".

If later materials claim that the window adjustment has been completed, they must be able to identify the corresponding entry point, review results, and rollback path. If all that appears is a new location, an old link, or a screenshot, it shows at most that the collaboration entry point has changed, not automatically that old materials and existing usage patterns remain compatible. This limitation is the boundary of this round's decision, not a judgment about outcomes that have not yet occurred.

See also the switchover handoff record for DOC-52. That material covers the handoff actions; this page retains the entry-point trade-offs, practical impact, options compared, and rollback boundaries. The two pages are not merged into a single comprehensive set of rules.

# Team Shared Entry Point Switching Handover Process

This handover is not about replacing one configuration path name with another. First determine who is still using the old entry point, then have a consumer that can roll itself back take on the first trial run. Without these two prerequisites, even if the candidate entry point appears usable locally, it cannot be handed to other modules as the shared entry point.

## The State Left by the Old Entry Point

The earliest records only followed the usage trail of `path-config` to find `src/configuration.ts`, and did not produce a complete caller table. Here, "old entry point" means the shared maintenance entry point already used by the team, while "candidate entry point" means the entry point prepared to replace it but still requiring validation by consumers. Neither can be assigned based solely on file location; locations in files may move during reorganization, and what actually needs to be handed over is the call relationship and rollback method.

The judgment retained from the old draft is: identify all consumers before discussing the switch. This judgment was not overturned by later review. The review added the fields needed for the handover, but did not turn unconfirmed callers, path names, or owning modules into established facts, so the sections below still use the old entry point, candidate entry point, and consumer list to represent the current-state objects.

When tracing back from `source-identity` to the actual entry point for "team shared entry point maintenance," continue with DOC-53. DOC-53 only handles locating the entry point; the switch order, failure branches, and rollback records remain on this page. Do not merge the two pages into a single code-reading guide.

## Establish the Inventory Before Handover

Maintainers should first create a consumer list. Each row corresponds to one real caller; do not count adjacent directories or modules that have only been mentioned. At minimum, retain the following columns:

| Item | Content to record |
| --- | --- |
| Consumer | A locatable call site or entry-point description |
| Current entry point | The old entry point it actually uses now |
| Candidate entry point | The object to replace during the trial; leave blank if unknown |
| Rollback action | Whether the consumer can restore the old entry point itself, and what state it restores to |
| Minimal reproduction | An input and observed result that can reproduce success or failure once |
| Owning module | Who owns the shared boundary when a boundary dispute arises |
| Migration batch | First trial, later batch, or deferred |

"Known consumers" does not mean "all possible consumers." Each located call entry must correspond to a row in the list; when you see only local clues such as `path` or `config`, record the clue first, and do not infer the consumer from the filename. An entry without an actual call entry cannot enter the first batch, and a generic label cannot substitute for one.

The list must also mark two reasons for deferral: first, the consumer cannot roll itself back; second, the cross-module boundary has not yet been confirmed. Deferral does not mean failure, nor does it mean migration is complete. They continue pointing to the old entry point until someone supplies a rollback action or completes the boundary confirmation.

## How to Run One Trial

The first batch contains only one consumer that can roll itself back. The reason for choosing it is not that it is "the most important," but that a failure will not take other consumers along to the candidate entry point. Before the trial, preserve the original record for the old entry point and write down this consumer's call entry and minimal reproduction; if the candidate entry point name has not been confirmed, the trial form cannot omit this field and can only remain in preparation.

Record the steps in the following order:

- First run the original input through the old entry point and save the smallest output that explains the result.
- Change only the entry point to which the first-batch consumer points; do not casually adjust the other consumers.
- Rerun the same minimal reproduction. Do not treat "it can start" as migration success; compare whether the call still reaches the expected shared boundary.
- If the result is abnormal, save the failure branch and the input that triggered it; do not change the candidate entry point first to hide the difference.
- If the result is normal, still perform a rollback, restore the consumer to the old entry point, and then confirm that the original reproduction still runs.

The rollback action itself is a deliverable of the first batch. Changing it over without changing it back cannot prove that this consumer Fang Ke took on the trial. If the old entry point cannot be restored after rollback, change the first-batch status to paused; other consumers must not enter subsequent batches.

## Do Not Merge Failure Branches

When the candidate entry point has a problem, leave separate traces for each symptom:

1. **Call entry not found.** First return to the old entry point; leave the candidate entry point blank or unconfirmed in the list, and do not treat a nearby file location as a replacement path.
2. **The call reaches the entry point, but the minimal reproduction produces a different result.** Preserve the old entry point's output and the candidate entry point's failure output, and mark the portions of the input that did not change. This is a compatibility problem with the candidate entry point; the consumer cannot be marked as migrated.
3. **The consumer cannot roll itself back.** Remove this consumer from the first batch and continue running it through the old entry point; the handover package should only record the missing rollback action and must not substitute an unconfirmed restoration step.
4. **Both modules believe the other is responsible.** Do not close this out using speculation from chat. Have the owner of the shared boundary confirm the owning module and write the confirmation back to the row; keep the status as migration in progress until confirmation.
5. **There is only a conclusion, with no minimal reproduction.** This record cannot advance the batch. Complete the triggering input, actual call entry, and failure branch, then review it again.

Failure records must allow another maintainer to distinguish between "the candidate entry point is incompatible" and "the consumer has not completed the handover." These two issues have different recovery targets: the former is handled by reverting the candidate entry point; the latter by adding the consumer's own rollback or confirming responsibility.

## Batches and Compatible Callers

The first batch contains only one consumer that can roll itself back. Only after the first batch completes "switch over—reproduce—roll back—reproduce again" can later batches be scheduled. Later batches must still be added one consumer at a time; do not switch the entire list at once. Each time a consumer is added, retain its original entry point, candidate entry point, minimal reproduction, and rollback action; success in the previous batch cannot let the next batch skip its own reproduction.

Callers with compatibility requirements should stay on the old entry point for now. Compatibility here does not mean "they all appear able to access it"; it means that both the caller's own call entry and its minimal reproduction produce acceptable results under the candidate entry point, and that it can return to the old entry point. A caller that has not completed all three items must be marked deferred, not migrated.

If a later batch exposes a shared-boundary problem, stop adding new consumers and handle only the row that has already been changed. Restore the old entry point first for anything that can roll back; for anything that cannot, leave the current status and owning module in place and wait for the boundary owner to confirm. Do not hand a failed caller over to an unconfirmed module just to keep the batch moving.

## Return to the Old Entry Point

Rollback is performed per consumer, rather than clearing all callers at once. First stop that consumer from continuing to trial the candidate entry point, restore the old entry point using the rollback action in the list, and then run its minimal reproduction. Only after the result is restored should you change that row from "first batch" or "later batch" to deferred. If the rollback action itself does not exist, do not assume that manually changing the path back is equivalent to restoration; leave the gap in the handover record and have the owning module provide an executable action.

The old entry point remains in place during migration. Keeping it does not mean acknowledging that the candidate entry point has failed; it provides a stable landing point for registered compatible callers that do not yet have rollback capability. Only when every entry in the consumer list has completed the four handover items—call entry, failure branch, minimal reproduction, and owning module—may you discuss closing the old entry point. If any item is still missing, the page remains in migration in progress.

## Minimum Contents of the Handover Package

Package the material given to the handoff recipient by consumer, rather than splitting it into several packages by file directory:

```text
Consumer:
Old entry point:
Candidate entry point:
Trial input:
Old entry point result:
Candidate entry point result:
Failure branch:
Rollback action:
Result after restoration:
Owning module:
Current batch:
```

Keep empty fields empty; do not fill them with "confirmed" or "no impact." In particular, for "candidate entry point result" and "result after restoration," do not write "passed" if they have not been run; for "owning module," write "pending confirmation" if the boundary has not been confirmed. The handover package can be brief, but it must tell the recipient which call entry to start from, which path to return to on failure, and who will handle cross-module disputes.

## Handover Status

| Status | Meaning | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pending inventory | Consumers and the old entry point have not yet been confirmed | Complete the list; do not switch |
| Trial pending | A consumer that can roll itself back has been found | Record the original reproduction, then trial the candidate entry point |
| Migration in progress | The entry point has been changed, but the four handover items are not yet complete | Complete the failure branch, minimal reproduction, or owning module |
| Eligible for later batches | The first-batch change and rollback can both be reproduced | Add the next consumer one at a time |
| Deferred | The caller is incompatible or cannot roll back | Keep the old entry point and fill the gap |
| Completed | This consumer's switch and rollback records are complete | Do not modify this row again |

"Completed" describes only one consumer; it does not mean that the shared entry point as a whole has been closed. The overall switch still depends on whether the list contains any pending-inventory, migration-in-progress, or deferred entries. If the page only has the candidate entry point name left, without a corresponding call entry and restoration record, continue to treat it as migration in progress.

# Postmortem: Team Shared Entry Point Maintenance Discrepancy

During the maintenance window, a recheck of the shared entry point showed that the new notice was visible, but access still led back to the old entry point. We initially thought the notice was just slow to refresh; after the second recheck, that explanation no longer held. The old entry point had not been removed.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Finding: new notice appears] --> B[Recheck: still reaches old entry point]
  B --> C[Remove new notice]
  C --> D[Keep old entry point]
```

The recorded impact was limited to people who had followed the new notice being sent back to the old entry point, and the original plan could not be completed by the end of the window. The coordinator retained the original execution records and checked what the entry point displayed separately from where it actually led.

The temporary recovery was to remove the new entry point notice while keeping the old entry point available. This eliminated the visible discrepancy but did not establish which step introduced it.

Still unknown:
- Where the original plan and the entry point configuration fell out of sync;
- Whether the original records can distinguish maintenance steps from configuration changes;
